TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention

Follow the cross-layer propagation of harmful semantics and intervene at the pathway level.

Shi Chuancheng

January 29, 2026 ·ICML 2026 ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

TraceRouter studies safety through paths connecting internal components. It localizes sensitive onset layers, uses sparse features to trace relevant attention interactions, and applies path-level suppression through a focused intervention. The goal is to interrupt the information flow associated with unsafe behavior while preserving general model utility.

The work evaluates both diffusion and language models, pairing safety measurements with quality or utility measurements. Its analysis shifts attention from where a feature exists to how that feature participates in downstream computation.

3Stages of pathway tracing
SAESparse feature isolation
FISIntervention-derived influence

A behavior can depend on a route through the network, making information flow a useful unit of intervention.

Why this matters

Distributed harmful computation can continue through multiple layers even when a local feature is suppressed. A defence therefore needs to examine how the information propagates.

How it works

  1. Locate a sensitive onset layer through attention-divergence analysis.
  2. Use SAEs and differential activations to isolate malicious features.
  3. Estimate feature influence with zero-out interventions and suppress selected downstream pathways.

What the study finds

Reported comparisons examine adversarial robustness together with general utility. The results support the value of tracing and suppressing selected propagation pathways rather than treating safety as a purely local feature intervention.

What this means

This gives interpretability a more relational target. Two components can matter because of the route linking them, even when neither isolated component fully explains the behavior. Tracing that route can make an intervention more specific about where and how it acts.

The practical challenge is selectivity across tasks and model families. Path-level evidence offers a way to reason about that selectivity, while the reported evaluations define the settings in which suppressing the selected routes improves safety with limited utility loss.
